title: Randomised Trials – Randomisation, ITT, Baseline Adjustment, Cluster and Non-Inferiority Designs

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A randomised controlled trial (RCT) assigns participants (or clusters) to interventions by a chance mechanism and compares their outcomes. Its design features protect that comparison:

  • Randomisation: the sequence of allocations is generated by chance. Simple randomisation assigns each participant independently (like a coin toss); block (restricted) randomisation guarantees equal numbers after every block of, say, 4; stratified randomisation uses separate blocked sequences within strata of a strong prognostic factor. Minimisation allocates each new participant to the arm that minimises the imbalance, summed over chosen prognostic factors, usually with a random element.
  • Allocation concealment: whoever enrols a participant cannot know or influence the next assignment until it is made.
  • Blinding (masking): participants, care providers or outcome assessors do not know the assigned arm.
  • Intention-to-treat (ITT): everyone randomised is analysed in the arm to which they were randomised, whatever they actually received. Per-protocol: only those who followed the protocol are analysed.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Randomisation is the reason RCTs can support causal conclusions (recall §11.5 and §11.6): chance, not the clinician or the patient, decides who gets what, so the arms are alike on average in both measured and unmeasured characteristics. Each other feature protects what randomisation achieves. Concealment stops a recruiter who knows the next allocation from steering sicker patients away from it; without it a trial can be subverted, and inadequate concealment “leads to exaggerated estimates of treatment effect, on average” (Schulz & Grimes, 2002). Blinding stops knowledge of the arm from changing care, reporting or outcome assessment. ITT keeps the randomised groups intact: dropping people who stopped treatment breaks the comparison that randomisation made fair, because those who stop usually differ from those who continue.

Randomisation balances groups on average, not in every trial. Simple randomisation of small trials can give unequal arms; block randomisation fixes the numbers; stratification and minimisation also balance chosen prognostic factors. Minimisation “provides better balanced treatment groups” than restricted or unrestricted randomisation and handles more factors than stratification (Scott et al., 2002; Pocock & Simon, 1975).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why simple randomisation can be unbalanced. With 20 participants and a fair coin, the number in arm A is binomial (n = 20, p = 0.5; recall §5.7.1.2). P(a split of 7:13 or worse) = 2 × P(X ≤ 7) = 0.26. One small trial in four is this unbalanced.

Blocks of 4. A block contains two A’s and two B’s in random order: C(4, 2) = 6 possible blocks (AABB, ABAB, ABBA, BAAB, BABA, BBAA; recall combinations, §5.7.1.2). After each block the arms are equal. A fixed block size can let a recruiter guess the last allocation of a block, so block sizes are often varied at random.

Adjusting for the baseline value. Let the outcome Y (say follow-up haemoglobin) and its baseline X have the same SD σ and correlation ρ. Three analyses compare arms on:

  • the final value Y: variance σ²;
  • the change Y − X: variance σ² + σ² − 2ρσ² = 2σ²(1 − ρ);
  • Y − βX with β chosen to minimise the variance, which is analysis of covariance (ANCOVA, a regression of Y on arm and X; recall §12.4): Var(Y − βX) = σ²(1 + β² − 2βρ), minimised at β = ρ, giving σ²(1 − ρ²).

Since 1 − ρ² ≤ 1 and 1 − ρ² ≤ 2(1 − ρ) for every ρ, ANCOVA has the smallest variance. The change score beats the final value only when ρ > 0.5. At ρ = 0.5 the variances are 1, 1 and 0.75 (× σ²); at ρ = 0.7 they are 1, 0.6 and 0.51. The sample size scales with the variance, so ANCOVA at ρ = 0.5 needs 25% fewer participants than either alternative.

Non-inferiority. Let d = new − standard (for cure proportions, higher is better) and let −M be the non-inferiority margin, the largest loss of efficacy that would still be acceptable. H₀: d ≤ −M; H₁: d > −M (recall §8.2). Reject H₀ at one-sided α = 0.025 if the lower limit of the one-sided 97.5% CI exceeds −M. That lower limit is the lower limit of the usual two-sided 95% CI, so: non-inferiority is shown if the whole 95% CI lies above −M. Equivalence needs the whole CI inside (−M, +M) (ICH, 1998).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Baseline adjustment. A simulated trial randomises 120 anaemic adolescent girls, in blocks of 4, to iron–folic acid (IFA) with counselling or to control, with a true effect of 0.4 g/dL. The simulation sets the baseline–follow-up correlation at about 0.6; this sample happens to give 0.70.

Non-inferiority. A new, shorter treatment regimen is compared with the standard, whose cure proportion is about 90%. Clinicians agree that a loss of up to 5 percentage points would be acceptable in exchange for the shorter course: M = 5 points.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Trial A, 600 per arm: cure 89.5% (new) vs 90.0% (standard). d = −0.5 points. SE = √(0.895 × 0.105/600 + 0.90 × 0.10/600) = √(0.0001566 + 0.0001500) = 0.0175, that is 1.75 points. 95% CI: −0.5 ± 1.96 × 1.75 = −3.9 to +2.9 points. The lower limit −3.9 lies above −5: non-inferior. The CI includes 0, so superiority is not shown.
  2. Trial B, 400 per arm: 88.0% vs 90.0%. d = −2.0; SE = 2.21 points; 95% CI −6.3 to +2.3. The lower limit is below −5: non-inferiority is not shown, although the CI includes 0. “No significant difference” is not non-inferiority.
  3. Scenario E of the figure: a CI of −4.6 to −0.4 is non-inferior (above −5) and yet significantly worse than the standard (below 0). Both statements are true; which matters depends on whether the margin was well chosen.

blocks.caption: Figure 15.11. Reading a non-inferiority trial from its 95% CI for the difference in cure proportion (new − standard), margin −5 points. A and B are computed in the Worked Calculation; C–E are illustrative.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
# simulated trial: 120 anaemic adolescent girls
set.seed(9)
# permuted blocks of 4
blocks <- replicate(30, sample(c("A", "A", "B", "B")))
arm <- factor(as.vector(blocks), labels = c("control", "IFA"))
table(arm)
# baseline Hb, g/dL
hb0 <- rnorm(120, 10.5, 1.0)
hb1 <- 10.5 + 0.6 * (hb0 - 10.5) + 0.4 * (arm == "IFA") +
  rnorm(120, 0, 0.8)
cor(hb0, hb1)
fits <- list(final  = lm(hb1 ~ arm),
             change = lm(I(hb1 - hb0) ~ arm),
             ancova = lm(hb1 ~ arm + hb0))
t(sapply(fits, function(f) round(coef(summary(f))["armIFA", 1:2], 3)))
arm
control     IFA 
     60      60 
[1] 0.6999205
       Estimate Std. Error
final     0.351      0.188
change    0.204      0.144
ancova    0.246      0.135

replicate(30, sample(...)) makes 30 shuffled blocks of AABB, so the arms end exactly 60:60. The sample correlation is 0.70. The three rows estimate the same true effect (0.4 g/dL) from the same girls. Their SEs, 0.188, 0.144 and 0.135, stand in the ratio 1 : 0.77 : 0.72, close to the √1 : √0.6 : √0.51 of the Derivation at ρ = 0.7. The estimates differ because, by chance, the IFA arm started 0.15 g/dL higher: the final-value analysis counts that head start as effect (0.351 = 0.204 + 0.146), the change score subtracts all of it, and ANCOVA adjusts by the fitted amount.

points.html: Do not test baseline differences. In a properly randomised trial every baseline difference is due to chance by definition, so a p-value for it tests a null that is known to be true. Such tests are “superfluous and could be harmful” (Schulz & Grimes, 2002) and “philosophically unsound” (Senn, 1994). Report baseline characteristics descriptively in Table 1, and adjust for prognostic variables named in the protocol whatever their baseline balance.

Prefer ANCOVA for a continuous outcome measured at baseline and follow-up. Vickers and Altman (2001): analysis of covariance is “the preferred general approach” and “generally has greater statistical power”; its gain over a change score is small when the correlation is high (say r > 0.8).

ITT is the primary analysis of a superiority trial, and it needs outcome data on everyone randomised; handle missing outcomes as in §15.4 rather than silently dropping people. A survey of trials in four major journals found ITT “often inadequately described and inadequately applied” (Hollis & Campbell, 1999). A per-protocol analysis estimates something different and loses the protection of randomisation.

In non-inferiority trials, ITT is not conservative. Dropouts in both arms tend to make the arms look alike, so the full analysis set “may be biased toward demonstrating equivalence” (ICH, 1998). Both ITT and per-protocol results are therefore usually reported, and non-inferiority is more convincing when both support it; CONSORT has an extension for non-inferiority and equivalence trials (Piaggio et al., 2012). The margin is fixed in advance on clinical grounds, and it must be smaller than the benefit the standard treatment is known to have, or “non-inferior” could mean no better than no treatment.

Cluster-randomised trials (villages, anganwadi centres, PHCs) are used when the intervention acts on a group or would contaminate neighbours. Plan the sample size with the design effect (§15.6 step 6) and analyse with methods that respect clustering: cluster-level summaries, mixed models or GEE (recall §15.2.4–15.2.5). Analysing individuals as if independent gives CIs that are too narrow. CONSORT has a cluster extension (Campbell et al., 2012).

Cross-over trials give each participant both treatments in random order, separated by a washout period, and compare within person, like the paired designs of §9.2.3. They suit stable chronic conditions and short-acting treatments. Watch for a period effect (outcomes differ by period whatever the treatment) and carry-over (the first treatment still acting in the second period).

Reporting. CONSORT 2025 (Hopewell et al., 2025), a 30-item checklist with a participant flow diagram, updates CONSORT 2010 (Schulz et al., 2010). Report the randomisation method, concealment, blinding, the sample size calculation (§15.6) and the analysis population.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.14

questions.prompt: A trial’s Table 1 reports baseline weight with “p = 0.04” and the authors write that “randomisation failed”. Explain why the p-value is the wrong tool and what the authors should do about a prognostically important imbalance.
questions.answer: If allocation was truly random and concealed, every baseline difference arose by chance, so the null hypothesis of the test is known to be true, and about 1 in 20 such tests will give p < 0.05 anyway (more when many variables are tested). A small p says nothing about whether randomisation failed; failure is judged from the process (sequence generation, concealment). What matters is whether an imbalance is large enough to affect the outcome, which depends on how prognostic the variable is, not on its p-value. The remedy is to adjust for prognostic baseline variables specified in the protocol (for example, by ANCOVA), whatever their balance, and to report baseline characteristics descriptively (Senn, 1994; Schulz & Grimes, 2002).

questions.prompt: In a planned trial of a salt-reduction intervention, the correlation between baseline and 6-month systolic BP is expected to be 0.6. A final-value analysis would need 200 participants per arm. Compute the variance factors for a change-score analysis and for ANCOVA, and the corresponding sample sizes per arm.
questions.answer: Relative to the final-value analysis (factor 1): change score: 2(1 − ρ) = 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 → 200 × 0.8 = 160 per arm; ANCOVA: 1 − ρ² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64 → 200 × 0.64 = 128 per arm. ANCOVA needs 36% fewer participants than a final-value analysis and 20% fewer than a change-score analysis.

questions.prompt: A non-inferiority trial of a community-based versus facility-based treatment for a childhood infection uses a margin of −10 percentage points. The ITT difference in cure is −3 points (95% CI −8.5 to +2.5); the per-protocol difference is −6 points (95% CI −11.8 to −0.2). What do you conclude, and why are both analyses reported?
questions.answer: ITT: the lower limit −8.5 lies above −10, so non-inferiority is shown. Per-protocol: the lower limit −11.8 lies below −10, so non-inferiority is not shown; the CI also lies wholly below 0, so community treatment was significantly worse among those who followed the protocol. The conclusion is that non-inferiority is not established. In a non-inferiority trial, ITT is not conservative: non-adherence and dropout in both arms make the arms look alike and bias the result towards non-inferiority (ICH, 1998). The per-protocol analysis loses the protection of randomisation, so its bias has no predictable direction; each covers the other’s weakness, so both are reported and a convincing claim needs both to agree.
